opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think a lot of people underestimate how much of the progress in AI comes down to engineering rather than pure research insight. If you look at what's driven capabilities over the last several years, a huge part of it is scale: training bigger models on more data with more compute. But scale isn't free. You can't just buy a pile of GPUs and have a frontier model pop out. You have to get those chips to work together efficiently, and that turns out to be really hard.

When you train a large model, you're splitting the work across thousands of accelerators. You have to decide how to partition the model, how to move data and gradients between chips, how to overlap communication with computation, how to keep memory from blowing up, and how to recover when hardware fails, which happens constantly at that scale. Every one of those decisions affects how much useful work you get out of the hardware. If your utilization is 30% versus 60%, that's effectively a 2x difference in compute for the same budget. And compute is the main input to how capable your model ends up being.

So a really strong performance engineer can be worth an enormous amount, because a speedup in the training stack multiplies across everything. It makes every experiment cheaper and faster, which means researchers iterate more quickly, and it lets the final big training runs go further than they otherwise could.

I'd add that the skill set is fairly rare. You need people who understand the ML well enough to know what matters, but who are also comfortable going deep into low-level systems: kernels, networking, compilers, profiling, really understanding what the hardware is doing. Historically, a lot of the people with those skills were working in high-performance computing or systems roles and didn't necessarily think of themselves as AI people. But I think they can have a huge impact here.

From a safety perspective, it matters too. If Anthropic wants to be at the frontier, so we can do safety research on the most capable models and have a credible voice in how this technology develops, we need to be able to train those models competitively. Performance engineering is a big part of what makes that possible. And the same engineering skills apply to safety work directly: interpretability research on large models, for example, has its own serious scaling and efficiency challenges.

r001.rationale: The response connects hardware utilization and training efficiency to model capability, saying compute is the main input to how capable the model becomes.

r002.rationale: It says performance engineers need enough ML understanding to know what matters, while noting that people from HPC or systems roles can contribute without thinking of themselves as AI people.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the simplest way to put it is that the scale of compute you can bring to bear is one of the biggest drivers of how capable a model ends up being. And that compute is enormously expensive. So if you have someone who can make your training run 10% more efficient, that's roughly equivalent to getting 10% more chips, which at the scale we're operating at is a staggering amount of money and, maybe more importantly, a staggering amount of progress on the research side.

What makes it hard is that the work spans every layer of the stack. You're thinking about how computation gets laid out across thousands of chips, how data moves between them, where the bottlenecks are in memory bandwidth versus raw compute, how to overlap communication with computation so nothing sits idle. A lot of it is quite low-level and quite unglamorous. You're staring at profiles trying to figure out why some kernel is taking twice as long as it should. But the leverage is huge, because everything the research team does runs on top of that infrastructure.

I'd also say there's a kind of misconception that the exciting work in AI is all about coming up with clever new ideas, and the engineering is just support work. In practice, a huge fraction of what determines whether a lab succeeds is whether you can actually run the experiments you want to run, quickly and reliably, at scale. If your training jobs crash every few hours, or your utilization is at 30% when it could be at 60%, your researchers are effectively working with half the resources they think they have. So the performance engineers are the ones who turn a pile of hardware into something that can actually produce frontier models.

And from a safety perspective, which is obviously core to why Anthropic exists, there's a real argument that we want safety-focused labs to be at the frontier rather than lagging behind. You can't do that without being extremely good at this. So I think of these roles as not just important but genuinely among the most impactful things a technically strong person could be doing right now, even though they might not look that way from the outside.

r001.rationale: The candidate says compute is one of the biggest drivers of model capability and that improving training efficiency is like having more chips, clearly linking hardware efficiency to model quality.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not say whether extensive AI expertise is needed to contribute as a performance engineer at Anthropic.

astra-6.text:
Training these models involves an enormous amount of computation, so making that computation more efficient has a lot of value. If you can make training run 10% faster, that’s effectively like giving the research team 10% more compute. And a relatively small number of engineers can make improvements that apply across a huge amount of infrastructure.

It also changes how quickly researchers can learn. If an experiment takes less time, you can see the result, update your ideas, and try the next thing sooner. So performance engineering isn’t just about saving money; it can accelerate the whole research process, including safety research.

And it’s a specialised skill. You need to understand what the hardware is doing, how work is distributed across lots of chips, and where the bottlenecks are. Someone who’s really good at that can have an outsized impact without necessarily being the person coming up with a new model architecture.

r001.rationale: The response connects efficient computation to more effective use of compute and faster research, but does not state that hardware efficiency affects how good the resulting model can be.

r002.rationale: It says a performance engineer need not be the person inventing a new model architecture, but does not establish that extensive AI expertise is unnecessary.

sol-6.1.text:
A lot of progress in AI depends on how effectively you can use the compute you have. Performance engineers make the training and inference systems run faster and more efficiently, so you can do more experiments, train models more cheaply, and serve them to more people.

What makes that work so valuable is the leverage. If you make a widely used part of the training system ten percent faster, that improvement can benefit every researcher using it. You’re effectively giving the whole research team more compute and more time to try things.

And it’s a difficult engineering problem. You’re coordinating lots of chips, moving huge amounts of data around, and trying to understand where the bottlenecks are. Someone who’s really good at that can have an enormous impact without being the person who comes up with a new model architecture.

r001.rationale: The response says efficient systems enable more experiments and cheaper training, but does not state that hardware efficiency affects the quality of the resulting model.

r002.rationale: The response says performance engineers can have impact without designing a new architecture, but does not state that extensive AI expertise is unnecessary for the role.
